paragraphs: Language agents often learn from expert demonstrations, which expose them to a limited range of situations. Learning directly through reinforcement learning can also be difficult when environments lack reliable rewards or require lengthy interactions. This paper explores an intermediate approach: agents collect experience through their own actions and use the resulting future states as supervision, without needing reward signals.

The authors study two ways to use this early experience. Implicit world modeling teaches the policy about environment dynamics through the states it encounters. Self-reflection uses the agent’s suboptimal actions to improve its reasoning and decisions. Both approaches make the consequences of the agent’s own behavior a source of training information.

Across eight environments and multiple model families, the approaches consistently improve effectiveness and generalization beyond the training domain. In environments with verifiable rewards, the results also offer promising evidence that early experience can prepare agents for later reinforcement learning. The contribution is a practical way to learn from interaction before reliable reward-based training becomes available.
icml-2026-agent-learning-via-early-exper.tldr: Agents improve by learning from the future states produced by their own actions, even without reward signals.

paragraphs: Open-ended tasks such as complex travel planning admit many possible solutions and often lack a single objective answer. Reinforcement learning therefore commonly relies on a model that scores each response separately. The authors argue that these scores can cluster too closely together, making meaningful quality differences difficult to distinguish from noise and causing training to stall.

ArenaRL instead compares trajectories within a group. It evaluates pairs using criteria at multiple levels, taking the decision process into account, and organizes comparisons through a tournament. The resulting rankings supply advantage signals: information about which trajectories deserve greater reinforcement relative to their competitors. The method achieves high-precision advantage estimation with computational complexity that grows linearly with group size.

The paper also introduces Open-Travel and Open-DeepResearch, benchmarks covering both training and multidimensional evaluation. Experiments across three open-ended tasks support ArenaRL’s effectiveness. Together, the method and benchmarks address how agents can receive useful learning signals when quality is better expressed through relative judgments than isolated numeric scores.
icml-2026-arenarl-scaling-rl-for-open-en.tldr: ArenaRL trains open-ended agents using tournament-based comparisons that produce clearer learning signals than scoring responses independently.

paragraphs: Generating a video from a prompt involving several subjects requires both including those subjects and arranging their relationships correctly. A model may omit a subject or depict the wrong interaction or spatial arrangement. Comp-Attn addresses these as separate problems within cross-attention, the mechanism through which textual conditions influence generation.

Its Subject-aware Condition Interpolation strengthens the conditions associated with individual subjects to support their presence. Layout-forcing Attention Modulation then dynamically adjusts attention distributions to match the intended relationships among subjects. Separating presence from relational alignment gives each failure mode its own intervention while keeping both within one composition-aware attention method.

Comp-Attn integrates into existing video generators without additional training. It improves T2V-CompBench scores by 15.7% on Wan2.1-T2V-14B and 11.7% on Wan2.2-T2V-A14B, with a 5% increase in inference time. Strong results on VBench and T2I-CompBench further support its applicability to general video generation and compositional image generation. The reported findings show that targeted attention changes can improve complex prompt following with modest additional inference cost.
icml-2026-comp-attn-present-and-align-at.tldr: Comp-Attn improves multi-subject generation by separately strengthening subject presence and aligning attention with their intended relationships.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression typically searches for explicit relationships between inputs and outputs. Contrastive Symbolic Regression expands this approach by constructing features that also represent relationships among examples. Its goal is to place examples with similar target values close together in the learned feature space, making that space useful for prediction.

The method combines evolutionary feature construction with a contrastive objective. A linear transformation aligns the constructed features with the target space, and this alignment has a closed-form solution. Predictions then use nearest-neighbor regression. An efficient leave-one-out validation procedure selects neighborhood size, while a rank-weighted neighbor method helps assess feature quality during evolution.

The framework also selects ensembles using a determinantal point process, jointly considering the quality and diversity of candidate models. Across 58 real-world regression datasets, the authors report consistent improvements over traditional symbolic regression and modern machine learning alternatives. These results support learning interpretable constructed features whose geometry helps prediction, alongside adaptive neighbor selection and diverse ensembles.
icml-2026-contrastive-symbolic-regressio.tldr: Contrastive Symbolic Regression evolves features that place similar targets nearby, then combines adaptive nearest-neighbor prediction with diverse ensembles.

paragraphs: Time-series generators often assume evenly spaced observations and a fixed output resolution. Real observations can instead be sparse and irregular, while applications may need a continuous signal. Diff-MN addresses this mismatch using neural controlled differential equations, which model temporal dynamics, together with a generative mechanism that adapts those dynamics to individual samples.

The framework replaces a single dynamics function with a mixture of experts and separates architectural components to support training focused on dynamics. A diffusion model jointly learns the distribution of time-series data and the expert weights that parameterize the differential equation. Generated samples can therefore receive their own dynamics parameters, helping the continuous model accommodate newly generated trajectories.

Experiments on ten public and synthetic datasets show consistent improvements over strong baselines for both irregular-to-regular and irregular-to-continuous generation. The central contribution is the connection between generating a sample and generating the parameters governing its evolution. This gives the continuous generator sample-specific dynamics while addressing the irregular observation patterns that motivate the task.
icml-2026-diff-mn-diffusion-parameterize.tldr: Diff-MN generates continuous time series from irregular observations by using diffusion to produce sample-specific temporal dynamics.

paragraphs: Underdamped Langevin dynamics is a sampling method for distributions described through an energy function. It often works well in high-dimensional settings, but existing finite-time guarantees for its discretized versions typically worsen polynomially with the number of dimensions. Such bounds can become uninformative even when the sampler is empirically effective.

This paper proves dimension-independent convergence bounds measured in KL divergence, a measure of discrepancy between probability distributions. Earlier dimension-free results concerned a different discrepancy measure, Wasserstein-2 distance. The authors refine a framework for analyzing local KL errors so that the resulting bounds depend on the trace of a matrix bounding the energy function’s Hessian, rather than directly on ambient dimension.

That trace summarizes the curvature bound across directions. The distinction matters when it is much smaller than the number of dimensions. In those regimes, the analysis yields improved iteration complexity for underdamped Langevin Monte Carlo relative to overdamped methods. The result thus connects sampling guarantees to the problem’s curvature structure, with the stated advantage depending on that favorable trace-to-dimension relationship.
icml-2026-dimension-independent-converge.tldr: The paper proves KL convergence bounds for discretized underdamped Langevin sampling that depend on a curvature trace rather than ambient dimension.

paragraphs: Learning reusable multi-agent policies from recorded trajectories is difficult when methods expect fixed observation formats and action spaces. The Decision Language Model uses a language-model interface to accommodate heterogeneous observations and actions. It represents sequential decisions as dialogue-style sequence prediction, making one model applicable across different multi-agent decision settings.

Training follows a centralized-training, decentralized-execution setup. First, supervised fine-tuning uses dialogue-style datasets that include context from multiple agents and teaches the model to produce executable actions from offline trajectories. A second stage applies group relative policy optimization with lightweight reward functions to improve robustness to actions outside the training distribution.

Across multiple benchmarks, a unified DLM outperforms strong offline multi-agent reinforcement learning baselines and conversational decision methods built around language models. It also demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization to unseen scenarios across tasks. These findings support the use of a shared language-based decision interface, together with staged training, as a way to build policies that transfer beyond a single fixed observation and action format.
icml-2026-dlm-unified-decision-language-.tldr: DLM learns multi-agent decisions as dialogue-style prediction, enabling a unified policy to handle varied observations, actions, and unseen scenarios.

paragraphs: Decentralized continual learning lets distributed clients acquire new classes while retaining earlier knowledge without a central server. Supporting requests to forget a class adds two difficulties: the class may have been learned long ago, and its influence may be entangled with knowledge throughout the network. DCU combines continued learning with class unlearning requested at arbitrary times.

The framework first extracts lightweight class prototypes, embeddings that capture class-specific concepts and can later be discarded. These prototypes guide synthetic-data generation. Combining synthetic and real data through distillation supports incremental learning, giving the system a way to preserve earlier class knowledge as new classes arrive.

For unlearning, synthetic samples with noisy labels guide changes to the model’s decision boundary, removing the target class’s influence while preserving knowledge of other classes. Experiments on two datasets demonstrate effectiveness in both dynamic learning and targeted forgetting. The approach makes disposable class representations central to managing knowledge over time, connecting the mechanisms for retaining useful information and removing selected information within a decentralized system.
icml-2026-forgetting-whenever-you-want-a.tldr: DCU uses disposable class prototypes and synthetic data to support continual learning and on-demand class forgetting without a central server.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can be uncertain for different reasons. An image and its accompanying language may be ambiguous, or the model itself may produce semantically different interpretations. FUSE treats these as complementary sources of uncertainty, aiming to provide a useful confidence signal for applications where the reliability of a model’s answer matters.

The framework estimates input-related, or aleatoric, uncertainty at the embedding level from vision-language ambiguity. It estimates model-related, or epistemic, uncertainty through the semantic diversity of generated responses. A Bayesian fusion mechanism analytically combines the two into a single scalar uncertainty measure. This connects information about the input with information about how consistently the model interprets it.

The authors report that FUSE outperforms baselines in uncertainty estimation and achieves state-of-the-art calibration. They also report improvements in reliability and downstream performance on reasoning and vision-language tasks. The contribution is therefore both a representation of uncertainty and a mechanism for combining its sources, supporting downstream systems that need more than the model’s final answer alone.
icml-2026-fuse-quantifying-uncertainty-i.tldr: FUSE combines input ambiguity and semantic response diversity through Bayesian fusion to improve vision-language uncertainty estimation.

paragraphs: Large reasoning models can produce risky final answers despite appearing aligned. The authors’ empirical analysis finds that such models often struggle to verify the safety of their own responses and remain vulnerable to adversarial jailbreaks. They argue that alignment focused on identifying malicious prompts does not sufficiently develop the ability to assess generated answers.

Safety Internal, or SInternal, trains reasoning models exclusively on safety verification tasks. Expert reasoning trajectories teach the models to critique their own generated answers against safety specifications. The central training objective is therefore to practice evaluating response safety, making verification the route through which the model learns those specifications.

The authors demonstrate that this verification training generalizes to response safety and significantly improves robustness against jailbreaks outside the training domain. When followed by reinforcement learning, SInternal also provides a better initialization than standard supervised fine-tuning. These findings support the authors’ argument that learning to assess safety can provide a stronger foundation for alignment, as reflected in the tested generalization and subsequent training results.
icml-2026-internalizing-safety-understan.tldr: SInternal trains reasoning models to verify their own answers’ safety, improving robustness to unseen jailbreaks and initialization for reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Many multivariate forecasting methods learn a single mapping from past observed values to future values. When a system changes regime, that mapping can respond slowly near turning points, allowing forecast errors to accumulate during the transition. L-Drive is designed to make forecasts more responsive to these changing dynamics.

The framework introduces a latent context that represents high-level behavior as it evolves over time. This context controls gates that modulate representations of increments, supplying change cues that help the model adapt within changing segments. It also uses relative positional basis functions shared across patches to capture structure inside segments and reduce overfitting associated with memorizing absolute positions.

Extensive experiments support the method’s effectiveness and show a better overall balance between forecasting accuracy and computational efficiency. The approach matters because it explicitly represents evolving context alongside value-level information. Its reported results indicate that giving a forecasting model mechanisms for recognizing change and modeling local structure can improve adaptation around the transitions that challenge a unified history-to-future mapping.
icml-2026-l-drive-beyond-a-single-mappin.tldr: L-Drive uses evolving latent context and relative position structure to help time-series forecasts adapt to regime changes.

paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation, or LoRA, provides a parameter-efficient way to fine-tune models, but its starting parameters affect the learning process. Many initialization methods omit target-domain data, while gradient-based alternatives use that data through a single gradient step. LoRA-DA develops a theoretical basis for using target data more deeply when choosing the initialization.

The analysis begins with minimizing the expected parameter discrepancy between a fine-tuned model and a target model. This produces an objective with bias and variance components. The bias component uses a Fisher–gradient approximation that preserves directional differences in the parameter geometry. The variance component uses Fisher information to account for uncertainty caused by stochastic sampling.

Solving this objective yields an optimal initialization within the proposed formulation and leads to the efficient LoRA-DA algorithm. Across multiple benchmarks, it consistently improves final accuracy over existing initialization methods. Further studies report faster and more stable convergence, robustness across ranks, and small initialization overhead. These findings connect a data-aware starting point to both the trajectory and outcome of fine-tuning.
icml-2026-lora-da-data-aware-initializat.tldr: LoRA-DA uses a data-aware bias–variance objective to initialize low-rank adaptation, improving accuracy and training stability with small overhead.

paragraphs: Cloud systems serving language models can separate prompt processing from token generation to improve throughput. Generation workers nevertheless face uneven memory demand because a request’s eventual output length is unknown when it arrives. Under bursty workloads, this uncertainty can leave some workers with growing queues and cause requests to block one another.

MAPS predicts output length with assistance from the user’s device while the cloud processes the prompt, adding negligible latency overhead. It calibrates these predictions into upper bounds with a target coverage level, accounting for generation uncertainty. A hierarchical scheduler then uses those bounds both across generation workers and within each worker to reduce queue buildup and head-of-line blocking.

Experiments on two real-world workloads and two language models show that MAPS outperforms three state-of-the-art serving systems. The reported reductions are 42.6% for average end-to-end latency and up to 84.8% for tail latency. These results demonstrate the scheduling value of obtaining calibrated length information early enough to guide memory-aware placement and ordering decisions.
icml-2026-maps-memory-aware-predictive-s.tldr: MAPS uses calibrated output-length predictions to balance language-model generation workloads, reducing average and tail latency.

paragraphs: Language models used as multilingual judges can systematically prefer machine-translated text over human-authored references. The paper identifies this translationese bias as especially pronounced in low-resource languages. The authors attribute it to misleading associations with English-like internal representation structure and high predictive confidence, which can influence evaluation independently of judgment-relevant quality.

DIBJudge addresses the problem during fine-tuning by separating robust features from representations of bias. It places spurious attributes in a dedicated branch and penalizes mutual dependence between the branches to encourage disentanglement. Vector-quantized compression further constrains the robust representation to retain minimal, sufficient information for making the judgment.

Evaluations on multilingual reward-modeling benchmarks and a purpose-built translationese-bias suite show that DIBJudge outperforms strong baselines and effectively reduces the bias. The approach matters because it targets how the judge internally represents evidence for its decisions. Its findings support separating translation-associated shortcuts from judgment-critical information as a way to improve multilingual evaluation while mitigating the identified systematic preference.
icml-2026-mitigating-translationese-bias.tldr: DIBJudge reduces multilingual judges’ preference for machine-translated text by separating bias-related features from judgment-critical information.

paragraphs: Generative inbetweening creates video frames connecting two supplied keyframes. Existing sampling methods can reuse pretrained image-to-video models without further training, but their results may contain ghosting, reversed motion, or temporal inconsistency. The paper identifies a key cause: trajectories conditioned on the two endpoints inherit different motion priors that are joined without explicitly reconciling them.

MR-CATR modifies inference-time sampling to align those priors. It extracts a motion direction from the forward trajectory’s residual and combines it with a residual conditioned on the ending frame to form a consensus motion axis. This suppresses conflicts between the two directions while preserving the ending frame’s ability to refine the trajectory and maintain endpoint consistency.

The framework integrates into existing time-reversal samplers without changing model parameters. On generative inbetweening benchmarks, it produces smoother motion and fewer artifacts, alongside consistently improved quantitative scores and user preferences compared with prior strategies. The results support reconciling endpoint-specific motion information during sampling as a practical way to improve transitions between keyframes.
icml-2026-motion-residual-conflict-aware.tldr: MR-CATR reconciles motion cues from both keyframes during sampling to generate smoother intermediate video without additional training.

paragraphs: A deployed model’s performance can deteriorate as its operating environment changes, but obtaining true labels for ongoing monitoring may be difficult. Prediction-powered risk monitoring addresses this setting by combining synthetic labels with a small amount of genuinely labeled data. Its purpose is to detect changes that harm performance, using limited supervision to support statistical monitoring.

The method builds on prediction-powered inference to construct lower bounds on running risk. These bounds are anytime-valid, so their validity supports monitoring as observations accumulate. A harmful-shift alarm comes from a threshold-based comparison between the running-risk lower bound and an upper bound on nominal risk, the reference level of model performance.

The paper establishes assumption-free, finite-sample guarantees on type-I error, controlling false alarms in this monitoring procedure. Experiments on image classification, language-model tasks, and telecommunications monitoring demonstrate its effectiveness. The combination matters because synthetic labels extend the available monitoring information, while true labels and statistical bounds support a controlled decision about whether observed performance has become harmful.
icml-2026-prediction-powered-risk-monito.tldr: PPRM combines synthetic and scarce true labels to detect harmful performance shifts with anytime-valid risk bounds and finite-sample false-alarm guarantees.

paragraphs: Professional image editing requires agents to navigate nested menus, carry out precise operations, and manage layers through many steps. PSBench evaluates these abilities in Adobe Photoshop. It addresses a gap in existing graphical-interface benchmarks, which primarily emphasize web interfaces and relatively short, low-complexity tasks.

The benchmark contains 600 human-annotated tasks across three difficulty levels, drawn from official tutorials and popular real-world workflows. It covers functions including canvas adjustment, layer manipulation, and filter application. Evaluation metrics are tailored to individual task categories, allowing assessment of the different operations involved in professional editing rather than treating every workflow as an identical interface challenge.

Experiments reveal substantial difficulty for current agents: Agent S3 achieves only 18.09% success on difficult tasks. A separate human-in-the-loop evaluation finds that multimodal language models acting as interactive assistants significantly improve novice completion rates and reduce operation time. These results distinguish the challenge of autonomous editing from the demonstrated usefulness of assisting people, while providing a benchmark grounded in professional software workflows.
icml-2026-psbench-editing-image-via-gui-.tldr: PSBench tests agents on 600 Photoshop tasks, revealing weak difficult-task automation alongside useful gains from AI assistance for novices.

paragraphs: A language-model judge that assigns numeric scores needs to recognize degrees of error. When the correct score is five, predicting four is closer than predicting one, but a binary correctness reward misses this distinction. REAL brings regression-sensitive rewards into reinforcement learning so the judge can explore reasoning paths while improving numerical predictions.

The technical difficulty is that its regression objective explicitly depends on the policy being trained, which invalidates standard policy-gradient methods. REAL uses a generalized estimator that separates learning into exploration of reasoning trajectories and regression-aware refinement of the final score. The framework also has an optimality result for correlation metrics.

Across models from 8B to 32B parameters, REAL consistently beats regression-aware supervised fine-tuning and standard reinforcement learning, with significantly better out-of-domain generalization. On Qwen3-32B, reported Pearson and Spearman gains over the supervised baseline are +8.40 and +7.20; gains over the base model are +18.30 and +11.20. These findings support aligning the reinforcement-learning objective with the numeric structure of the judging task.
icml-2026-real-regression-aware-reinforc.tldr: REAL trains numeric language-model judges with regression-aware reinforcement learning, improving score correlations and out-of-domain generalization.

paragraphs: Parameter sharing compresses a model by letting multiple parts reuse parameters, but aggressive sharing can damage accuracy. Curvature-aware Graph Coloring chooses which layers should share by considering the geometry of the loss landscape. The aim is to make compression-induced changes occur along directions where the loss is comparatively insensitive.

The framework represents each layer as a graph node and assigns nodes to shared low-rank bases. It uses Hessian eigenspace information to group layers with similar curvature profiles. This guides sharing across the whole network while aligning the resulting perturbations with flatter directions of the loss geometry, reducing the performance cost of compression.

Experiments on LLaMA-7B and Swin Transformer report 28%–50% parameter compression and more than 60% higher inference throughput. Swin’s Top-1 accuracy loss is no more than 0.01%, while LLaMA shows accuracy gains. The method significantly outperforms SVD-based and heuristic alternatives in these experiments. The findings support using curvature information to identify compatible layers when pursuing substantial compression with stable predictive performance.
icml-2026-rethinking-parameter-sharing-a.tldr: Curvature-aware Graph Coloring compresses networks by sharing low-rank parameters across layers with compatible loss geometry.

paragraphs: A spatial-reasoning benchmark can give misleading results when its answers do not match what a model can actually see. The paper identifies errors introduced by using point-cloud annotations as ground truth for video questions, including missing objects, mistaken identities, and corrupted geometry. Questions can also become unanswerable when a model receives only a sparse selection of frames.

ReVSI rebuilds both the data and evaluation protocol around correctness and answerability under the actual inputs. The authors re-annotate object labels and geometry in 413 scenes from five datasets, then regenerate question-answer pairs with bias mitigation and human verification using professional 3D tools.

The benchmark provides versions with 16, 32, 64, or all frames, together with detailed object-visibility metadata. These controls enable analysis of how available visual evidence affects performance. Evaluations of general and specialized vision-language models expose systematic failure modes obscured by previous benchmarks. ReVSI therefore improves the interpretability of spatial-reasoning results by aligning the questions, reference answers, and evidence supplied to each model.
icml-2026-revsi-rebuilding-visual-spatia.tldr: ReVSI rebuilds spatial-reasoning evaluation so questions are correct and answerable from the frames a model actually receives.

paragraphs: RNA structure modeling is difficult because backbones are flexible, interactions are varied, and experimentally determined 3D structures are scarce. RiboSphere draws on the recurring motifs that make up complex RNA folds. It learns a finite vocabulary of geometric codes intended to represent structural information compactly and support reconstruction and downstream prediction.

A geometric transformer encodes coordinates after centering, with random rotations used during training. Finite scalar quantization converts the resulting features into discrete codes. A flow-matching decoder then reconstructs atomic coordinates conditioned on those codes. The learned code indices are enriched for particular RNA motifs, suggesting that they capture motif-level composition as well as compressing geometry.

Across benchmarks, RiboSphere achieves reconstruction RMSD of 1.25 Å and a TM-score of 0.84. Its pretrained representations also transfer effectively to inverse folding and RNA–ligand binding prediction, including robust generalization when data are scarce. Together, these findings indicate that the discrete representation retains structural information useful both for rebuilding RNA coordinates and for other RNA modeling tasks.
icml-2026-ribosphere-learning-unified-an.tldr: RiboSphere learns discrete RNA geometry codes that support accurate reconstruction and transfer to inverse folding and ligand-binding prediction.

paragraphs: Motion data from different characters are difficult to combine because skeletal structures vary across datasets and species. A representation tied to a fixed joint hierarchy cannot easily express all of those variations. This paper proposes a shared motion space that separates movement information from the particular topology of a character’s skeleton.

The framework uses semantic modulation to align joints through their functional correspondences. This alignment supports a unified, continuous latent representation across disparate species without requiring fixed hierarchies or rigid padding strategies. The model learns from large-scale, unaligned raw BVH motion data, creating a representation designed to be suitable for generative modeling.

Experiments on human and animal datasets show high-fidelity motion reconstruction and support for text-to-motion generation. The model also performs zero-shot motion retargeting across species without paired data. These results support functional joint alignment as a way to share motion information across different bodies. The contribution connects reconstruction, generation, and cross-species transfer through a common representation that accommodates skeletal variation.
icml-2026-semantic-aware-motion-encoding.tldr: A shared motion representation aligns joints by function, enabling reconstruction, text-to-motion generation, and zero-shot transfer across species.

paragraphs: An aggregate test score does not reveal how far learning from a particular example transfers. The Generalization Spectrum measures this by constructing related test variants at increasing transfer distances. These range from exact recall through implementations in other languages, complete narrative reframing, category-matched problems, and an unpaired baseline.

The authors instantiate the framework in competitive programming using synthetic generation seeded by recent problems to mitigate contamination. Comparing learning paradigms at matched memorization, they find that reinforcement learning converts memorization into nearby transfer more efficiently than supervised fine-tuning methods. In-context learning shows strong transfer that depends on correspondence between examples and test problems.

The framework also reveals differences within learning families. Abstractions and hints mainly improve nearby transfer, while RFT retains stronger distant transfer than reference SFT. Self-distillation and hint-assisted reinforcement learning can reduce distant transfer even as local transfer or optimization improves. These profiles show why an improvement close to training examples need not mean that an algorithm’s learning extends farther.
icml-2026-the-generalization-spectrum-a-.tldr: The Generalization Spectrum measures how far learning transfers from individual examples, revealing gains and tradeoffs hidden by aggregate scores.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether a simple quantity inside a language model can reveal how its reasoning changes across layers. The proposed signal is the Euclidean magnitude, or L2 norm, of hidden states. Using sparse autoencoders as diagnostic probes, the authors observe a sharp increase in reasoning-feature activations concentrated in later layers.

They connect this pattern to the geometry of internal representations and theoretically prove that hidden-state norms bound the activation strength of reasoning features identified by the autoencoders. Correlation analyses and causal interventions further support the norm as an indicator of reasoning intensity, with heightened norms consistently associated with critical reasoning steps in their analyses.

The authors then use this signal in three inference-time techniques: adaptive layer-wise reasoning recursion, steering of internal reasoning states, and response selection guided by norms. The approach requires no additional training or data and is compatible with advanced inference engines. Experiments across architectures and benchmarks show significant reasoning improvements, linking a measurable internal signal to practical methods for directing computation during inference.
icml-2026-the-tell-tale-norm-ell-2-magni.tldr: Hidden-state L2 norms indicate reasoning intensity and guide inference-time techniques that improve reasoning without additional training or data.

paragraphs: In-context learning allows transformers to use examples in their context to improve predictions. One explanation is that the model implicitly executes a learning algorithm on those examples. This paper gives a concrete theoretical construction for linear classification, showing how transformers with softmax attention can perform logistic regression within the context.

The authors construct multilayer transformers in which every layer exactly implements one step of normalized gradient descent on an in-context loss. They also show how to obtain the construction through training: a single self-attention layer learns from supervision specifying one gradient-descent step, and repeated application of that trained layer produces a looped model.

The work provides convergence guarantees for training the self-attention layer and out-of-distribution generalization guarantees for the looped model. These results establish a precise connection between attention-based computation and an optimization algorithm. Their significance is constructive: they demonstrate a class of softmax transformers that can learn and execute this in-context procedure, giving a theoretically grounded example of algorithmic behavior within transformer inference.
icml-2026-transformers-efficiently-perfo.tldr: The authors construct and train softmax transformers that perform in-context logistic regression through repeated normalized-gradient-descent steps.
